summary: AARNet Engineering Note 001: naming guidelines for the AARNet X.500 Directory Service, recording current or proposed practice at the Australian Academic and Research Network.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a set of rules a university network in Australia wrote for how to give names in their phone-book system.

questions: what is a dsa in x.500
how are australian organisations named in x.500
subtitle: How the Australian research network names organisations, people and servers in its X.500 directory.

tldr.problem: Internet guidelines for naming entries in X.500 directories differ from the Australian national standard, and AARNet wanted to follow the national one.
tldr.mechanism: AARNet places states and territories, organisations and residents under c=AU following Standards Australia, and puts all directory servers under a pseudo organisation called DMD.
tldr.outcome: The note records where AARNet departs from the Internet naming guidelines of RFC 1384. It is informational.

today: RFC 1562 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It documents AARNet practice from December 1993.

sections.title: Purpose and Alignment
sections.content:
This is AARNet Engineering Note AEN-001 from the Australian Academic and Research Network, which takes part in the global Internet X.500 based Directory Service. Its audience is administrators of an X.500 Directory System Agent (DSA).

AARNet generally follows RFCs that alter or supplement the X.500 standards. Where they conflict with its national standards body, Standards Australia, it aligns with the national body. For naming, this note records the difference from the Internet guidelines in RFC 1384.
sections.plainLanguage: This note is for the people who run the phone-book servers. It says where Australia does things its own way.

sections.title: States, Servers and Organisations
sections.content:
The Standards Australia document allows only two kinds of object directly below the c=AU node: organisations with nationally recognised names, and localities for the states and territories. AARNet adds one modification: ADMD and PRMD names are treated like organisations with nationally recognised names.

The eight states and territories are locality entries named with the stateOrProvinceName attribute, using the standard two or three letter abbreviations. Organisations with a name unique within Australia may go directly under the Australian entry. If the name is unique only within a state or territory, it must go under that state entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The country is the top drawer, states are drawers inside it, and each organisation goes in the drawer where its name is one of a kind.

sections.title: Server Names and Naming Rules
sections.content:
Naming organisational DSAs directly under the country node leads to clutter. To avoid it, and to conform to Standards Australia requirements, AARNet created a pseudo organisation called DMD where all Australian DSAs should be registered. It suggests naming DSAs after Australian fauna.

An organisation's distinguished name must be its officially registered name, at most 64 characters, though more familiar names can be added as additional names to aid searching. Residents are placed under their state, with a name made from their common name and street address.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers go in their own back room so the front of the phone book stays tidy. Each group is listed by its real name, and nicknames can be added so people find it.

references.text: Barker P., and S. Hardcastle-Kille, "Naming Guidelines for Directory Pilots", RFC 1384, January 1993.
Standards Australia: Naming and addressing in the Australian OSI Environment. SAA MP59-1991.
